extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of detective fiction; readers of Edgar Allan Poe; writers interested in realistic investigative detail
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles of realistic investigation and evidentiary reasoning as illustrated in a detective-narrative (Poe's The Mystery of Marie Rogêt). Useful for literary analysis or for writers aiming for plausible investigative plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider collateral and circumstantial events
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the least usual error ... is the limiting of inquiry to the immediate, with total disregard of the collateral or circumstantial events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dupin argues that a large portion of truth arises from seemingly irrelevant or incidental events; investigators should divert inquiry from the immediate event to contemporary circumstances (newspapers, related occurrences) because collateral facts often yield the most valuable clues. Example: rather than confining to the corpse itself, survey public prints for minute points that establish a direction for inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify affidavits and alibis beyond doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: We will ascertain beyond a doubt the validity of the affidavits in regard to his whereabouts on the Sunday. Affidavits of this character are readily made matter of mystification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do personal inquiry to validate alibis; do not accept written statements at face value because they can be fabricated or misleading. Example: Dupin re-examines St. Eustache's affidavits as a necessary early step in eliminating suspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine newspapers and public prints broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: I will examine the newspapers more generally than you have as yet done. ... a comprehensive survey of the public prints will not afford us some minute points which shall establish a direction for inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically search multiple periodicals and press reports (not just the most obvious item) for details, inconsistencies, and collateral reports that can suggest lines of inquiry. The press may contain both useful facts and misleading repetitions; extract fresh or overlooked particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of suggestion shaping public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: When arising of itself—when manifesting itself in a strictly spontaneous manner—we should look upon it as analogous with that intuition... it is important that we find no palpable traces of suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether 'public opinion' is genuinely spontaneous or has been prompted by planted stories/communications; suggested opinion is unreliable. Example: a known outrage nearby influenced the populace to assume a gang for the unknown case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check environmental plausibility of physical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no real evidence ... that the articles discovered had been more than a very few days in the thicket ... touching that mildew ... is he really unaware of the nature of this mildew? Is he to be told that it is one of the many classes of fungus, of which the most ordinary feature is its upspringing and decadence within twenty-four hours?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of natural processes (mildew, grass growth, local traffic) and local geography to judge whether items plausibly could have been where claimed for the alleged period. Example: grass can grow inches in a day; mildew/fungi change appearance rapidly—claims of weeks-old decay may be erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether evidence arrangement is natural or staged
rubrics_metrics.description: Here is just such an arrangement as would naturally be made by a not over-acute person wishing to dispose the articles naturally. But it is by no means a really natural arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine placement and ordering of objects for signs of artificial arrangement (items neatly placed on stones, 'shelf-like' positions) versus the disorder expected from a real struggle (trampled, scattered). Artificially arranged evidence may indicate planting to divert attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply material-mechanics knowledge (e.g., fabric tearing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pieces, as described, do indeed 'look like strips torn off;' but purposely and by hand. It is one of the rarest of accidents that a piece is 'torn off' ... To tear a piece from the interior ... could only be effected by a miracle through the agency of thorns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical, material knowledge about how objects behave (how fabric tears, effect of thorns, hem structure) to evaluate whether forensic descriptions are plausible. Specifics: tearing from interior requires two forces and is unlikely by thorn; hemmed edges resist being torn off—claims should match physical possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer number of assailants from nature of the struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: What struggle could have taken place—what struggle so violent and so enduring as to have left its 'traces' in all directions—between a weak and defenceless girl and the gang of ruffians imagined? The silent grasp of a few rough arms and all would have been over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether traces of struggle (extent, duration, dispersion) fit an encounter with multiple attackers or a single determined assailant. A brief overpowering by many would leave different signs than a prolonged single struggle; use logical plausibility to deduce likely number of perpetrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer perpetrator type from evidence left behind
rubrics_metrics.description: There was sufficient presence of mind (it is supposed) to remove the corpse; and yet a more positive evidence than the corpse itself ... is allowed to lie conspicuously in the scene of the outrage—I allude to the handkerchief with the name of the deceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the behavior implied by the evidence (leaving a named handkerchief, failing to remove other incriminating items) is consistent with a gang or an individual. Groups are more likely to remove incriminating items; individuals may be panic-stricken and leave things behind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret traces of body handling (dragging vs lifting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Between the thicket and the river, the rails of the fences were found taken down, and the ground bore evident traces of some heavy burden having been dragged along it!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific manner in which a body was moved (drag marks, rails taken down, uses of improvised handles/hitches) to infer whether it was transported by one person (who might improvise a handle, drag the body) or by multiple persons (who would lift and be unlikely to drag or dismantle fences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize expert/medical inferences for evidentiary basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The surgeon's published inferences, in regard to the number of ruffians, have been properly ridiculed as unjust and totally baseless, by all the reputable anatomists of Paris.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept authoritative-sounding forensic conclusions without examining the underlying evidence and reasoning; experts may overreach. Cross-check anatomical/forensic claims with other specialists or observable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming causation from coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It would have been a miracle indeed, if ... there should have been another similar gang ... engaged in a wrong of precisely the same aspect, at precisely the same period of time!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the intuitive leap that simultaneous or similar events must have a common cause; evaluate probabilistic plausibility before linking incidents. Similarities may be coincidental or may reflect suggestion rather than common authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider victim's intentions and tactical behavior (e.g., elopement)
rubrics_metrics.description: She must have foreseen the chagrin of St. Eustache ... She must have foreseen ... If it were my design to return at all ... I will tell St. Eustache not to call for me until dark ... If it were my design never to return ... the gaining of time is the only point about which I need give myself any concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing events, model the possible plans and intentions of the victim (deceptions to avoid immediate detection, instructions given to others) because these choices affect expected timelines and evidence. Use plausible motive-and-behavior reasoning to generate alternative hypotheses (elopement vs. abduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for local human habits affecting discovery of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: This thicket ... was in the immediate vicinity, within a few rods, of the dwelling of Madame Deluc, whose boys were in the habit of closely examining the shrubberies ... It is exceedingly hard to comprehend how the articles could have remained in this thicket undiscovered, for a longer period than one or two days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the routine behaviors of local inhabitants (children playing, gardeners, frequent passersby) when judging whether objects could have remained undiscovered. Local usage and customs can make alleged long-term concealment implausible.
